name: Scapula Waste
description: Scapula Waste is a flat, shoulder-blade-shaped world whose profile from orbit is remarkably asymmetric, one hemisphere significantly higher in elevation than the other. The high side is a plateau of wind-scoured stone, while the low side is covered in fine grey dust that fills ancient impact basins to their rims. A system of canyons connects the two hemispheres, carved by long-vanished water into sinuous channels now dry as bone.

The thin atmosphere carries just enough pressure to support wind, and that wind is relentless. It drives the grey dust in low, creeping waves across the flatlands, gradually burying and revealing surface features in cycles that span decades. The sky is a faded pink during the day, darkening to black at the edges where the atmosphere thins to nothing. Sound travels poorly, giving every noise a muffled, distant quality.

Ruins of geometric precision have been found half-buried in the dust seas, their surfaces carved with patterns that repeat at multiple scales in fractal arrangements. The ruins are made of a ceramic material not found naturally on the planet and show no signs of weathering despite their estimated age of over a million years. Microbial life thrives in the dust itself, feeding on minerals and moisture deposited by the thin atmosphere, seemingly unrelated to whatever civilization left the ruins.

The fractal patterns in the ruins have generated intense academic interest, with some mathematicians claiming they encode information in a format not yet decoded. Expeditions to excavate the buried structures are complicated by the constant dust migration, which can bury or reveal sites unpredictably. The microbial ecosystem produces silicon compounds of unusual purity that have modest industrial value, providing economic justification for maintaining a presence on an otherwise desolate world.
